events.notes:
Claude found some good material, and I think the best version is a merge rather than picking one draft. **Its strongest additions are the juvenile-ID honesty, the formal 1994 naming story, and the fruit-fiber detail. Mine had the better “Peach River is a real place” hook and a cleaner visitor-facing structure.**

A few factual notes first. *Archontophoenix tuckeri* is accepted by Kew and was formally published in 1994. Lucid gives the type locality as Upper Peach River, Bonanza Creek, collected in 1948, and describes a palm to about 20 m / 65 ft with new leaves often bronze-red, a waxy light- to lime-green crownshaft, and silvery-scaled leaflet undersides. ([Plants of the World Online][1])

I would **keep “Peach River” front and center**. That is more relatable than “named for Robert Tucker” as an early-page fact. The naming story is interesting, but it is secondary.

The current teaser:

> Its new fronds flush pink to bronze before greening — and the lime crownshaft that replaces them is like nothing else in the palm family.

I would change. “Like nothing else in the palm family” is much too strong, and crownshafts are common across palms. Better:

> **The “Peach River” in the name is a real place: the specimen used to describe this species was collected beside Upper Peach River in far northern Queensland.**

That is distinctive, true, and different from the first At a Glance.

For `at_a_glance`, I’d merge our two drafts into something like:

```xml
<at_a_glance>
  <block>
    <text>New leaves often emerge bronze, reddish or pink before maturing to deep green. The colour is brief, so catching one at its best is partly luck.</text>
  </block>

  <block>
    <text>Turn over a leaflet and the green disappears: the underside is silver-grey from a dense layer of tiny scales.</text>
  </block>

  <block>
    <text>The species was only formally named in 1994, even though the specimen that anchors the name had been collected beside Upper Peach River in 1948.</text>
  </blo
